subject: paul-bettany
research_tasks: Draft must treat the Depp texts (C25, C26) neutrally: quote exact words with outlet and date, state Depp's denial and both trials' outcomes, and do not infer motive from the jokes.
Do not state an Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars appearance; recheck casting status before any refresh (review trigger on C33).
Father's coming-out age conflicts (Bettany: 63; Telegraph 2013: 75). Attribute to Bettany or omit the number.
If space allows, open the original 2012 Guardian, 2013 Guardian, 2020 Total Film and 2026 Times interviews (paywalled or blocked here) to replace the secondary relays S03, S08, S21, S28.
Reverify podcast quotes (S23) against the audio timestamps before drafting; the transcript is machine-generated.

sources.title: Paul Bettany (The Times interview by Tim Teeman, author repost)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Tim Teeman
sources.locator: Margin Call press interview; paragraphs on school, Matthew, cocaine, therapy, fame (author archive repost of The Times piece)
sources.excerpt: "I was a really bullied kid," ... "My godfather was gay and I would challenge every homophobic comment I heard. Consequently I had the shit kicked out of me because they thought I was gay." ... "It was a heart- breaking, alienating experience. I felt like I was harbouring this huge secret. I was so fragile." ... "I stopped because it was threatening my ability to act: the one thing that gave me self-worth." ... "God yes, four years on and off. In a world absent of Jesus, it's the flawed, but solitary option." ... He remains "full of self-doubt — I do not operate from a place of certainty". ... "But you shouldn't be sustained by other people's adulation. What if it goes away?"
sources.context: Long-form Times interview over lunch in New York, age 40, promoting Margin Call. Covers dyslexia and bullying, Matthew's death at 8 when Paul was 16, early-20s cocaine addiction ("work kept me on an even keel"), the 9/11 phone calls to Connelly, therapy, and fame. Teeman notes it is "all said without self-pity". Also: "Making Margin Call 'was the first amazing artistic experience I'd had in years' ... 'It made me think I can't be a gun for hire any more.'" Text read on the author's archive; the original Times page was not opened.

sources.title: Paul Bettany interview: this time it's serious (The Telegraph, Celia Walden)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Celia Walden
sources.locator: Full article via Wayback raw capture; paragraphs on lateness, son's birth and money, school bullying, 9/11, addiction, death
sources.excerpt: 'I have a pathological fear of being late' ... 'Suddenly I thought to myself, "---- all this. The world is precarious and I'm going to make my children as safe as possible – with dough." And I went about doing that. It was ludicrous, of course, because they were safe. ... but there I was hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming. It sounds neurotic, but it's not, because the tap can turn off.' ... 'I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone' ... 'My experience of addiction was very much linked to a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was' ... 'I felt so uneducated. Those people were supersized to me and I was always trying to proximate the way they constructed their sentences.' ... 'I worry about death in general a lot.'
sources.context: Interview at the Chateau Marmont while shooting Transcendence, promoting Blood (2013). Walden reports he tries not to be away from family for longer than two weeks, that after 9/11 he rang Connelly for days ("Why have I been calling this woman for three days?"), and that the marriage gave him "a certainty that was new to me". She also reports his father "aged 75 ... announced his bisexuality", which conflicts with Bettany's later "came out at 63". The bullying at Chancellors school predates Matthew's death. Walden was warned he would not discuss his brother that day.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on How He Rekindled His Love for Acting (Daily Actor, relaying The Guardian)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, quoted from a Guardian interview
sources.locator: Second and third paragraphs quoting the Guardian Blood interview
sources.excerpt: "Acting used to be somewhere I could put loads of terrible feelings and bad experiences and try to make something creative out of them. But then I married and had children and everything got eclipsed. I know how precarious life can be, so I then had a period when I was making as much money as I could, so my children would be safe. Then I made a film called Margin Call, which was shot in two weeks on a low budget."
sources.context: Daily Actor summary of a 2013 Guardian interview about Blood. The Guardian original could not be opened (crawler blocked), so this is a secondary relay; the same safety-through-money account appears independently in S02 two weeks earlier and in S01.

sources.title: Interview: Paul Bettany On Creation (CinemaBlend)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Q&A answer on whether he was nervous acting with Connelly
sources.excerpt: My heartbeat tends to lower when cameras are on. I tend to get much calmer. I'm anxious in everyday life. I'm anxious about my kids' health, my health, whether I"m going to get the job I want, the chicken's going to turn out all right, the dog's going to poop in front of the paparazzi.
sources.context: Roundtable-style junket interview for Creation, in which he played Darwin opposite Connelly. Delivered with jokes; the interviewer calls him "as lively and funny as you might expect". He adds that on Master and Commander he could hold bugs once the camera rolled though he "fucking hate[s] bugs".

sources.title: Paul Bettany on why his directorial debut is about homelessness (The Independent, Kaleem Aftab)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Kaleem Aftab
sources.locator: Paragraphs on the film's theme, busking, and his father
sources.excerpt: "But I didn't want to make a film about homelessness," he insists. "I wanted it to be about judgment." ... "It's just that people are eminently forgivable." ... "My father, who has just died, was a very religious man," says Bettany. "I'm not. I was raised a Catholic and he used to say this thing whenever we passed a homeless person, 'There but for the grace of God, go I.' Although I'm not a religious man, I love that sentence. There is an admission of how easily it can be us."
sources.context: Interview about Shelter (2014), which he wrote and directed and which stars Connelly. The story was inspired by a homeless couple outside his New York home. He says his busking past probably fed the film but "I didn't want it to become part of a narrative in discussing the film". Connelly, he says, "is incredibly honest about my artistic endeavours – brutally so."

sources.title: Paul Bettany talks 'Uncle Frank' and his own closeted father (Windy City Times)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Q&A answer to whether he was reluctant to accept the role
sources.excerpt: But the first question I had for Alan was "Why me?," and I [followed that] with "Should I even do this?" ... My father, because of the dogma of Catholicism, went back into the closet. He was arguably with the love of his life and when my father died—in my arms!—I found in his pocket a glass vial of Andy's ashes. ... My father had some beautifully curated stories and anecdotes, but I never really got to know him because he didn't live his life in an authentic way.
sources.context: Phone Q&A for Uncle Frank (2020), in which he plays a closeted gay professor. He says he asked himself whether it was "morally correct" to take the role and whether he had "the energy" to "think of some dark moments in your life". He and director Alan Ball found they shared "early traumas in our lives and deaths of our siblings".

sources.title: Exclusive Interview: Paul Bettany ... shares a touching story about his father coming out late in life (The Queer Review)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Quoted answer in the article body (accompanying video interview)
sources.excerpt: "It was really why I decided I had something to offer," Paul Bettany told The Queer Review. ... "So for me, it was a question of being able to imagine what if my father had got right with himself and could have had the happy ending that Frank and Wally get in this story? So that's why I did it and that's why it was important to me."
sources.context: Independent outlet, separate interview from S06 the same week; confirms the father account (came out at 63, about 20 years with Andy, back into the closet, the vial of ashes).

sources.title: Paul Bettany Says His Gay Father Went Back Into The Closet in His 80s (Out, relaying Total Film and NewNowNext)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via Total Film); Alan Ball (via NewNowNext)
sources.locator: Body paragraphs quoting Total Film, then Alan Ball
sources.excerpt: "He came out of the closet at 63. He then had a 20-year relationship with a man called Andy Clark. It was a joyous relief for everybody, actually." ... "The shame he felt for his sexual identity was devastating, he was unable to mourn the person who I think was the love of his life." ... "We talked about it a lot, and the fact we both had very traumatic experiences in our adolescence and how those stayed with us," Ball explained. "For Paul, the movie became a chance for him to have his own 'what if' story about his father. What if he was able to really embrace who he was and live his life fully?"
sources.context: Secondary relay of a Total Film interview and of director Alan Ball's NewNowNext interview; neither original was opened. PinkNews (same day) relays the same quotes, so it is not independent corroboration. Ball's remark is named third-party testimony about why Bettany took the role.

sources.title: WandaVision's Paul Bettany Says Watching His Father Struggle with His Sexuality Shaped Him as a Dad (People, via Yahoo)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: People magazine interview excerpt, paragraphs on childhood and father
sources.excerpt: "I was a sort of fool at home in front of my parents, but then at school very bashful," he says. "I was the kid that didn't go out at recess." ... "I thought I'd be dead on a couch by 25. ... But you grow up." ... "I really want my children, and I want everybody, to just live authentically as the person they are, and however hard that is, it's absolutely better than pretending to be something other than you are." ... "Having been through a thousand years of therapy, there's real power in getting to know yourself ... and I have so many things to be grateful for," he says.
sources.context: People magazine WandaVision cover-week interview. The magazine says he coped with Matthew's death "by drinking and partying" before drama school at 19.

sources.title: WandaVision's Paul Bettany Says His Marriage to Jennifer Connelly 'Really Altered Who I Was' (People, via Yahoo)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: People interview excerpt, paragraphs on marriage and family
sources.excerpt: "Yeah, totally faked my way into that one; poor Jennifer, as she slowly realized how ill-educated I was," he jokes. ... "Marriage and children changed my life," says Bettany. "It really altered who I was and what I saw as my goals." ... the moments that mean the most to the actor are "when I catch myself and realize the five of us are laughing together," he says.
sources.context: Companion People excerpt from the same WandaVision interview as S09. People restates that he realised he loved Connelly "after frantically worrying about her" after 9/11 and proposed before they dated.

sources.title: Paul Bettany says having his texts with Johnny Depp about Amber Heard made public was 'a strange moment' (Yahoo Entertainment, relaying The Independent)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via The Independent)
sources.locator: Paragraphs quoting the Independent interview
sources.excerpt: "It was a strange moment," he said of being involved in Depp's legal battle. "What was strange about it was you suddenly have one of the most scabrous newspapers in London and their lawyers poring through your texts for the last 10 years. Can you imagine what it would be like, honestly, to have a bunch of lawyers go through every one of your emails and texts for 10 years? All I can tell you was that it was an unpleasant feeling." ... "I don't feel that I signed some Faustian pact with the devil when I became an actor to give away all my privacy."
sources.context: Secondary relay of a December 2021 Independent interview (original not opened). He says "I think that I just pour fuel on the fire" by discussing it, and recalls a filmed subway argument with Connelly that led to divorce rumours reaching his children's school.

sources.title: Paul Bettany says it was 'embarrassing' to have texts with Johnny Depp shared during court trial (Insider, via Yahoo)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via The Times); text messages read in court
sources.locator: Article body: text exchange as read in court; Times quotes; 2016 tweet
sources.excerpt: In a series of texts, Depp wrote, "Let's burn Amber!!!" to which Bettany responded: "Having thought it through I don't think we should burn Amber — she's delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I'm not sure she's a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments — we do a drowning test. Thoughts?" ... "We live in a world without context," he said. "I didn't know Johnny when he was married to Amber. I knew him before. But we hadn't spoken for years." ... "I know how this works. Anything that you say is oxygen for a fire. And there's just no fucking fire," he added. ... In a tweet in 2016, Bettany said: "Known Johnny Depp for years and through several relationships. He's the sweetest, kindest, gentlest man that I've ever known. Just saying."
sources.context: Insider report on a February 2022 Times interview given before The Collaboration opened at the Young Vic. The 2013 messages were read in Depp's 2020 UK libel case against The Sun's publisher (which Depp lost) and resurfaced in his 2022 US trial against Amber Heard. The wording of the texts varies slightly between outlets. The Times original was not opened.

sources.title: The Personal Testimony of Paul (The Rake, Nick Scott)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Nick Scott
sources.locator: Opening paragraphs (preview text; remainder of feature not visible)
sources.excerpt: "Hang on... Where is it, where is it? I've just got to check my talking points... " "Talking points?" "'Don't mention the war' stuff. Things I'm not supposed to say. There's always a list. When I did press for The Da Vinci Code, in which I played an albino Catholic murderous monk, I was told I couldn't talk about albinism, Catholicism or murder. Hilarious."
sources.context: Zoom cover interview for A Very British Scandal. Only the opening was accessible. Scott writes that "Having to be judicious about what he says to strangers, though, doesn't quite chime with his innate candour. Bettany, you see, is no closed book."

sources.title: Paul Bettany on fame, playing the game, and staying sane (Gentleman's Journal, Joseph Bullmore)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Joseph Bullmore
sources.locator: Hour-long Zoom interview; sections on emotion access, fame, isolation, "Finish strong", neurosis
sources.excerpt: "Some people have amazing access to their emotions, and can switch them on like that," ... "And I'm just not good enough to do that." ... "if I find myself in a scene that requires that, I find myself picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at," ... "But it's spurious and I have watched it, with myself, come and go — it's an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it." ... "You're certainly not meeting the actual me, and I'm not meeting who you really are." ... "What I have realised is that I do better than I think in isolation," he says. "I'm quite convivial and social, and so I'm always surprised to see how well I do with my own company. I feel like I shouldn't have the personal resources to be on my own at all. I feel like I should fall apart more than I do. But I don't." ... "It's irritatingly industrious of me. But I have that ethos myself, when I'm up at work and tired and against it." ... "I'm not any less neurotic now, by the way" he says before we go. "I'm just better at hiding it."
sources.context: Interview from a cabin near his Vermont house for the film of The Collaboration. Also: Talking about acting "is like talking about sex"; the Lennon lyric "makes me feel less alone and alienated in the world"; a fan asked for a selfie while he stood crying after hearing his father was gravely ill. The journalist calls Stellan "the oldest" of the children; Kai, Connelly's son, is older.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on playing Warhol, family ghosts, and how therapy 'saved' him (The Daily Beast, Tim Teeman, author repost)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Tim Teeman
sources.locator: Zoom interview during the Broadway run of The Collaboration; sections on fear, bullying, father, therapy, work ethic, career slump, Depp, citizenship
sources.excerpt: "For instance, with Andy Warhol, it's his fear. I was very bullied as a schoolkid, and I remember the world feeling like a frightening place. I try to remember that in me." ... "I wouldn't take part in any of the homophobic banter around me, and the consequence of that, well you can imagine… I sort of refused to bend on that." ... "It's more that I have a really strong work ethic. ... The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day." ... "I couldn't just fall apart. What was making me feel safe and relevant was my career, rather like Warhol. Then my children came along, and all of that disappeared like mist." ... "We had kids, suddenly we had a fucking mortgage. I thought, what if this thing comes tumbling down?" ... "I said to him, 'Look, this town is full of second and third acts, and you should mind your fucking manners.' I walked out. My legs went because I acted so tough!" ... "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits," ... "I am so much less certain and definitive about things." ... "I refuse to put more fuel on this fire that's just been really unpleasant."
sources.context: Daily Beast interview reposted on the author's site. Also: therapy "absolutely saved me" and is "like having a chronic injury" needing upkeep or "you lean back into old patterns"; "I was very lost for a number of years, but there were always something that saved me or people that saved me"; politics occupies him "to an unhealthy extent"; he took US citizenship because he "was tired of getting shouted down on Twitter for having an opinion". Teeman reports the father died "aged 86 in 2015" and Bettany says his father came out "when he was 63". Bettany declined to discuss the Depp texts further.

sources.title: Paul Bettany explores being art star Andy Warhol on Broadway (AP, Mark Kennedy, via KTVZ)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany; Kwame Kwei-Armah (director)
sources.locator: AP feature body; director quote mid-article
sources.excerpt: "I don't know how you get underneath the wig and the glasses and the carefully curated public persona. I don't know how to do it," Bettany recalled thinking. ... "Paul did this brilliantly as an actor, I think. We introduced the Andy that we know, and then he just opens more doors and more doors and more doors into the land of imagination," says Kwame Kwei-Armah, the play's director. ... "All I want to do is be with people and get it out of me. So I'm not sure it's the healthiest thing in the world for me, frankly, but I love the doing of it."
sources.context: AP wire profile syndicated by KTVZ; independent reporting from the Daily Beast piece. Kwei-Armah's comment is named professional testimony about his craft, not his motives.

sources.title: Jennifer Connelly on Being Directed by Husband Paul Bettany (E! News, relaying DuJour)
sources.speaker: Jennifer Connelly (via DuJour)
sources.locator: Article body quoting Connelly's DuJour April 2014 cover interview
sources.excerpt: "It was kind of strange, going to work in the morning with the director," ... "But it really seemed to come quite naturally to him—phew—and it was an amazing experience to have had together." ... "I had this fantasy that we'd talk about scenes all day," Connelly recalls. "In reality, if the man sat down, there was a line of people wanting to talk to him. Since we moved so quickly, I think he felt his wife was the least of his worries."
sources.context: Named testimony from his wife about working under him on Shelter, relayed by E! from DuJour. Light and promotional; not evidence of inner motive.

sources.title: 'WandaVision': Elizabeth Olsen Says She and Co-Star Paul Bettany Have 1 Thing In Common (Showbiz Cheat Sheet, relaying Grazia)
sources.speaker: Elizabeth Olsen (via Grazia)
sources.locator: Final section quoting Olsen's Grazia interview
sources.excerpt: Olsen says that they work well together because they share a trait in their approach to the work: "He's very precise, like me."
sources.context: Co-star testimony relayed from Grazia; the Grazia original was not opened. Short and work-focused.

sources.title: Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany Test Their Real-Life Chemistry (Interview magazine)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany and Elizabeth Olsen
sources.locator: Conversation transcript; Bettany answers on the November 2020 election and on what is next (read via r.jina.ai)
sources.excerpt: I've been watching television for about 23 hours a day, and my wife [the actor [Jennifer Connelly](https://www.interviewmagazine.com/film/jennifer-connelly-claudia-llosa-aloft-sundance-2015)] is furious at me. She's like, "Could you just stop watching television for five minutes?" ... God, I really don't know. Gainfully unemployed. Right now it's just lovely hanging out with the kids, but at some point I'm going to actually have to think about paying the mortgage.
sources.context: The two co-stars interviewing each other before WandaVision premiered, recorded just after the 2020 US election result. Jokey register throughout.

sources.title: Paul Bettany says Marvel transformed his life after he was told his career was over (Reuters, syndicated by Devdiscourse)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, speaking to Reuters
sources.locator: Reuters wire text, VisionQuest London premiere red carpet
sources.excerpt: "It means I have been able to not take jobs and spend time with my family. It means that I've been able to direct and write a movie." ... "I was doing an audition with a producer who will remain nameless, who told me my career was over," he said. "I got up, I walked out, I went downstairs and my legs gave way. I sat on Sunset Boulevard and I went, you know what, maybe he's right, maybe my career is over," Bettany said.
sources.context: Reuters interview at the London premiere of VisionQuest (Monday, 12 October 2026), syndicated without edits. Notes VisionQuest completes the trilogy begun with WandaVision (2021) and Agatha All Along (2024). The syndicated text contains invisible zero-width characters inside some words; they are removed from the excerpt.

sources.title: Paul Bettany addresses 'Burn Amber' texts with Johnny Depp: 'Haven't spoken to him since' (Gulf News, relaying The Times)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via The Times)
sources.locator: Article body quoting the Times interview published Thursday 15 October 2026
sources.excerpt: "I hadn't spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven't spoken to him since. I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn't spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the s--- two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd," he said. "So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me. I've been married 23 years [to actress Jennifer Connelly] and, for what I do, I live an incredibly quiet life," Bettany added. "Everybody kind of thought this is probably a nothing burger — and left it alone."
sources.context: Secondary report of a VisionQuest-era Times interview (original not opened). Gulf News notes the 2016 X/Twitter post praising Depp "appears to have disappeared when Bettany left the platform", and that he discussed the texts with The Times in 2022. Other 2026 outlets report boycott calls against VisionQuest over the texts.

sources.title: Paul Bettany recalls struggle with guilt over brother's death (Rova, wire copy)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via Sibling Revelry podcast)
sources.locator: Wire summary of the Sibling Revelry episode released 13 October 2026
sources.excerpt: "It was really incredibly hard. He fell off, I guess he was playing hide and seek and he fell off a building that I had taught him how to climb. So there was an enormous amount of guilt to work through on that," Bettany added.
sources.context: Wire write-up of the podcast; the episode audio itself was opened and transcribed as S23, which is the locator of record. The wire copy says the family lived on the grounds of Queenswood School, where Thane Bettany taught drama.

sources.title: This is Paul Bettany (Sibling Revelry with Kate Hudson and Oliver Hudson)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, with Kate Hudson and Oliver Hudson
sources.locator: Episode audio (52:40), RSS enclosure; timestamps: 11:50-12:30 career worry; 13:30-14:20 safety net; 20:50-22:30 punctuality; 22:40-26:10 Matthew, guilt, maze, therapy; 27:58-29:50 music vs acting mask; 30:18-33:25 father; 41:00-42:50 9/11; 44:30-45:08 Proust
sources.excerpt: [11:55] "Oh, yeah, I don't think that ever ends, no. Which is really depressing. But I am better at relaxing into taking downtime. But after a couple of months, I start to go, I wonder if anybody remembers me." ... [14:05] "my dad was always like you gotta have a second string to your bow and mine was acting that was my my safety net" ... [21:10] "So the notion of always building more time to be there stuck with me." ... [22:20] "i'm an absolute fascist about being on time" ... [23:22] "he fell off a building that I had taught him how to climb. So there was an enormous amount of guilt to work through on that." ... "everybody is sort of dropped into a maze by their childhood. And the job of growing up is trying to find your way, you know, out of, out of that maze." ... [24:30] "When I was in crisis, I was just too busy trying to stay on the earth, you know." ... [28:10] "cause I hated playing my songs. I felt so revealed, hated it." ... "But I'm not sure I want anybody to really know that much about me definitively." ... "and there was always a mask that I could hide behind, even if it, even if I was playing a character that was exactly like me, nobody knew" ... "I also don't want to sort of trade on the, the trauma and, and, and drama of it all." ... [32:35] "he had to get into heaven as a straight man so he could see his son who had died" ... [42:00] "no word of a lie about 48 hours trying to ring Jennifer." ... [45:00] "watching the light die in her eyes as she realized I hadn't actually read Proust."
sources.context: Sibling Revelry episode released 13 October 2026, the day before VisionQuest premiered; hosts Kate and Oliver Hudson, Bettany speaking from New York. Audio downloaded from the public RSS enclosure and transcribed locally (whisper small.en for the whole episode; the quoted clips re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo, which agreed). The conversation has three voices and no speaker labels, so only lines that answer a question put to Bettany are attributed; nearby remarks about actors needing approval and validation are not attributed to him. Both models heard "couldn't turn very negative things into something creative" where the sense suggests "could"; that phrase is not quoted. The 9/11 account here says "about 48 hours" of calling; the 2013 Telegraph has "three days". He attributes the lyric "Mother, you had me, but I never had you" to "Sean Lennon"; it is John Lennon's "Mother". He says his father came out "at 63", consistent with his 2020 and 2022 accounts.

sources.title: Paul Bettany: the man, the Marvel (Square Mile, Max Williams)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Max Williams
sources.locator: Q&A sections on WandaVision line, busking, Gangster No. 1, set discipline, the producer story
sources.excerpt: PB: It didn't happen like that. It was an incredibly collaborative process with Jac, and she would bring both me and Lizzie [Elizabeth Olsen] into the conversations. We all knew what the line had to carry, but I kept pushing back because I didn't feel like we were quite there yet. ... we thought it would be for the weirdos. I count myself as one of them. ... "If you're five minutes early, you're late. Know your lines. Be bold – the theatre gods will come to your aid." I really believe in that. ... But having an idea, a plan, and something you understand where you are in the story… otherwise, what are you doing? You're just like a performing monkey unless you have a plan for how to tell the story. ... When I went in for the audition, nobody knew who I was, so I pretended I was a right ruffian. That made everybody feel safe enough to offer me the job. ... I had no expectations to succeed.
sources.context: VisionQuest-era cover interview. Also: busking "wasn't romantic at all ... The further away from that time I got, the happier I was"; asked "Do you know who you are and what your purpose is?" he answers "Some days!"; the tattoo naming Jennifer and the children; "I was very jovial, jokey, and wanting to have fun" on A Knight's Tale; he hopes to "write and direct again". The intro states the swansong question; he says decisions are "for people further up the food chain".

sources.title: VisionQuest: Paul Bettany and Terry Matalas Talk Ultron's Return, Mindspaces, and Robot Families (Den of Geek)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany; Terry Matalas (showrunner)
sources.locator: Feature quotes from Bettany and Matalas
sources.excerpt: "I haven't really troubled myself with trying to play a robot because they give me a costume and prosthetics that make me look like a robot. I'm quite lazy, so if the job's done for me by the costume and makeup, then I get on with the stuff I have to do," Bettany laughs. ... "This is a show about grandfathers, fathers, and sons," the actor muses.
sources.context: Pre-premiere press feature. Matalas: "It was vital that Paul have someone of equal adult stature to play off against". Bettany says he rewatched Vision's earlier appearances "to remember his mindset".

sources.title: The MCU series VisionQuest will explore "intergenerational pain with lasers" (Popverse)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, Space Con 2025 panel
sources.locator: Panel quote paragraph
sources.excerpt: "My show is about intergenerational pain with lasers. And a lot of jokes. That's what it is. Fathers and sons and stuff."
sources.context: Convention panel remark while VisionQuest was in post-production; jokey register.

sources.title: Paul Bettany (Wikipedia)
sources.speaker: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: Infobox; Early life; Career; Personal life
sources.excerpt: Paul Bettany (born 27 May 1971) is an English actor. ... When Bettany was 16, his brother Matthew died at age 8 after falling onto concrete from a tennis pavilion roof at Queenswood. ... On 1 January 2003, Bettany married American actress Jennifer Connelly in Scotland, whom he met when they starred together in the 2001 film A Beautiful Mind.
sources.context: Used only for biographical scaffolding (birth date, marriage date, filmography, Emmy nomination for WandaVision, Drama Centre London from 1990). Wikipedia lists him for Avengers: Secret Wars (2027); that is not independently confirmed here and should not be stated as fact.

sources.title: "That was the end of family life from that point" - When Paul Bettany opened up about his brother's death (Sportskeeda, relaying a 2012 Guardian interview)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via The Guardian, 2012)
sources.locator: Quoted Guardian passages in article body
sources.excerpt: "My brother's death, when he was eight years old, blew the family apart. He had an accident, and it was miserable. It coloured everything. I was 16, and that was the end of family life from that point, as often happens in families where's there's a death of a child. The whole family explodes." ... "You feel like you are harbouring some dreadful secret about what life is actually like."
sources.context: Aggregator relay of a Guardian interview (original not opened). Wording overlaps S01's "harbouring this huge secret", and the Telegraph (S02) quotes the same "blew the family apart" line as something he "has said", so the substance is corroborated by two opened outlets.

claims.claim: Bettany's younger brother Matthew died at age 8 after falling from a tennis pavilion roof at the school where their father taught; Paul was 16, and he says the death "blew the family apart".
claims.inference: A dated, repeatedly told formative loss; it establishes the circumstance every later safety-seeking choice has to be weighed against.
claims.alternative: Grief and trauma alone can produce lifelong hypervigilance in any type; this event cannot by itself show type.

claims.claim: In October 2026 he said Matthew fell from a building "that I had taught him how to climb", leaving "an enormous amount of guilt to work through".
claims.inference: Adds a self-blame strand that later interviews show being worked through in therapy; useful as a late, specific disclosure rather than as type proof.
claims.alternative: Survivor guilt after a sibling death is common and circumstantial; it does not discriminate between 6 and 4.

claims.claim: He describes fear as predating the brother's death: a "really shy kid", bullied at school, who says "I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone" and remembers "the world feeling like a frightening place".
claims.inference: Fearfulness reported before the 16-year-old's trauma weakens a trauma-only explanation of his later vigilance and supports an anxious baseline.
claims.alternative: Bullying is itself a circumstance; the fear may be situational to that school rather than temperamental.

claims.claim: At school he refused to join homophobic banter and challenged it, and was beaten for it; he says "I sort of refused to bend on that."
claims.inference: Taking a costly stand for a threatened in-group (his gay godfather, father's world) fits a loyal, counterphobic Six pattern of standing firm against the threat.
claims.alternative: Could equally reflect Four identification with outsiders, or simple moral conviction; it does not by itself discriminate.

claims.claim: After Matthew's death he left school, moved to London and busked; in his early twenties he became addicted to cocaine, which he linked to "a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was".
claims.inference: His own diagnosis of the addiction is about missing foundation, i.e. security and grounding.
claims.alternative: "Not knowing who I was" is also classic Four identity language; this passage cuts both ways.

claims.claim: He says he quit cocaine because it threatened his ability to act, "the one thing that gave me self-worth", and that "work kept me on an even keel".
claims.inference: Work functioned as a stabilising structure; he chose the structure over the drug.
claims.alternative: A Three reading (worth through work) also fits this line; the later rejection of praise as a measure (C12) weighs against that.

claims.claim: After 9/11, while staying in Italy (Tuscany in his 2012-2013 accounts, Umbria in 2026), he spent days phoning Jennifer Connelly in New York until he realised he loved her, then proposed before they had dated; he later said the marriage gave him "a certainty that was new to me".
claims.inference: A threat to someone he cared about produced checking behaviour and then a commitment that he describes in terms of certainty: a security move.
claims.alternative: Crisis-driven romantic clarity is common in many types; the "certainty" phrase is a journalist's paraphrase-adjacent quote from one interview.

claims.claim: When his son was born he decided "the world is precarious" and set out to make his children "as safe as possible – with dough", taking studio jobs for money; he called it "hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming".
claims.inference: The clearest repeated, costly choice: he traded artistic preference for financial security, while recognising the threat was exaggerated. This is the main Six discriminator against Four.
claims.alternative: Ordinary parental prudence, and an actor's incentive to justify commercial roles in hindsight; a Four could make the same trade under pressure.

claims.claim: After making Margin Call (2011) cheaply, he said "I can't be a gun for hire any more" and that the film reminded him what he loved about acting.
claims.inference: Shows the security strategy was revisable once a safer footing existed; meaning returned after safety.
claims.alternative: This return to artistic meaning is the strongest Four-compatible turn in the record.

claims.claim: He frames his professional discipline as control over uncertainty: "The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day"; he has a "pathological fear of being late"; he passes on the advice "If you're five minutes early, you're late."
claims.inference: Preparation as a hedge against what cannot be controlled, repeated across 2013, 2022 and 2026.
claims.alternative: Professional craft norms and British punctuality; Olsen's "precise" remark could reflect training rather than anxiety.

claims.claim: He describes himself as chronically anxious and uncertain: "I'm anxious in everyday life"; "I do not operate from a place of certainty"; "I'm not any less neurotic now ... I'm just better at hiding it."
claims.inference: Consistent first-person anxiety across 2010, 2012 and 2022, including the observation that he becomes calmer once the camera (action) starts.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecating anxiety talk is also a British comic register and a junket habit; self-report cannot show the motive is core.

claims.claim: He treats fame and praise as unreliable supports: "What if it goes away?" (2012); "it's an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it" (2022); judging yourself by others' praise is one of the "terrible, terrible things" about the job.
claims.inference: Distrust of an external support, framed as a security question, argues against a Three reading and fits Six scepticism.
claims.alternative: A Four also distrusts fame because it misrecognises the "actual me" (C18).

claims.claim: He says he worries about death "a lot", feels terror when his children jump on the couch, and finds 25-year product guarantees sobering.
claims.inference: Threat-scanning focused on the safety of loved ones, consistent with a Six attention pattern.
claims.alternative: Directly traceable to Matthew's fall; circumstance may explain it fully.

claims.claim: Around the 2008 crash, with "a fucking mortgage", he thought "what if this thing comes tumbling down?" and called his career what "was making me feel safe and relevant".
claims.inference: Explicit safety language attached to work and money, a decade after C08.
claims.alternative: Financial worry after 2008 was widespread and circumstantial.

claims.claim: When a producer told him his career was over, he says he answered "you should mind your fucking manners", walked out, and his legs gave way because "I acted so tough"; minutes later Joss Whedon called offering Vision. Later tellings vary in detail.
claims.inference: Bravado in the face of a threat followed by collapse is the counterphobic Six sequence in miniature; he tells it against himself.
claims.alternative: A polished, much-repeated anecdote shaped for audiences; details shift between versions (middle finger, sitting on the pavement), so treat it as self-mythology with a stable core.

claims.claim: He has been in therapy for years ("four years on and off" in 2012; "a thousand years" by 2021-2022) and says it "absolutely saved me", comparing it to treating a chronic injury so you do not "lean back into old patterns".
claims.inference: Long reliance on a trusted support structure and maintenance mindset.
claims.alternative: Therapy use is common across types and among actors; it shows self-work, not type.

claims.claim: He says family keeps him steady: "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits"; he tries not to be away more than about two weeks; Marvel money means he can turn down jobs to be with family.
claims.inference: Family as the secure base that regulates him, repeated 2013-2026.
claims.alternative: Devoted-parent statements are standard press fare and fit many types.

claims.claim: He also speaks in Four-like terms of alienation and authenticity: after Matthew's death he felt he was "harbouring some dreadful secret about what life is actually like"; fans are "not meeting the actual me"; he counts himself among "the weirdos".
claims.inference: This is the strongest evidence for the Four alternative and must be shown honestly.
claims.alternative: The alienation passages describe grief and fame encounters, not a cultivated identity of difference; elsewhere he deflates his own artistic self-image (C19).

claims.claim: He repeatedly deflates talk about his own artistry: he apologises for "sounding like a ponce when I talk about acting"; it is "like talking about sex"; he is "quite lazy" about playing a robot; he says others access emotion more easily and "I'm just not good enough to do that."
claims.inference: A Four typically invests in the artist-self and its emotional depth; Bettany treats his own as faintly embarrassing and frames emotion access as a technique he must work at.
claims.alternative: Could be British self-deprecation or junket modesty rather than motive.

claims.claim: To cry on camera he describes "picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at", keeping talismans of his brother (including Matthew's sweatshirt on Uncle Frank) near the set.
claims.inference: Shows he uses grief deliberately as a work tool and then questions it ("What the hell am I doing!").
claims.alternative: Using personal pain in art is a Four-compatible behaviour; the method framing is also standard actor training (Drama Centre London).

claims.claim: His father Thane came out to him at 63 (Bettany's account), lived about 20 years with Andy Clark, then went back into the closet for his Catholic faith after Andy died; when Thane died, a vial of Andy's ashes was in his pocket. Bettany says he "never really got to know him".
claims.inference: A father who lived inauthentically for safety is a central family story and the background to his Uncle Frank, Warhol and VisionQuest comments.
claims.alternative: Dates conflict: Telegraph 2013 says Thane announced bisexuality "aged 75". Use Bettany's own account, attributed, and avoid exact ages beyond what he says.

claims.claim: From his father's retreat into the closet he drew a parenting rule: "I really want my children ... to just live authentically as the person they are".
claims.inference: Value statement; supports the Four alternative's authenticity theme and also a Six-style protective vow for the next generation.
claims.alternative: Parenting values statements in People magazine are low-cost signals.

claims.claim: He hesitated over Uncle Frank, asking "Why me?" and "Should I even do this?"; director Alan Ball said the film became Paul's "what if" story about his father.
claims.inference: Doubt-first engagement with an offer, then commitment once a reason is found; Ball's testimony places the motive in repairing the father story.
claims.alternative: The hesitation is partly the 2020 debate about straight actors in gay roles, which he names.

claims.claim: He questioned whether he could play Warhol at all, then built the role around Warhol's fear: "with Andy Warhol, it's his fear. I was very bullied as a schoolkid".
claims.inference: Fear is the doorway he chooses into another person.
claims.alternative: Actors routinely link roles to their past in press; this is interpretation of a role, not of himself.

claims.claim: He is wary of how statements are used against him: on the Depp texts, "Anything that you say is oxygen for a fire" (2022) and "whatever I say becomes a click link" (2022); in 2026 he said he "decided to say nothing", though he had commented in 2021 and 2022.
claims.inference: Threat-anticipating caution about public speech, plus a small contradiction between "say nothing" and his earlier comments.
claims.alternative: Normal crisis-PR caution for any celebrity; the contradiction may be compression by the 2026 interviewer.
claims.review_trigger: New statements by Bettany, Depp or Heard about the texts; any change in the 2026 VisionQuest boycott story; publication of the full Times 2026 interview.

claims.claim: In 2013 text messages read in Depp's 2020 UK libel case, Bettany replied to Depp's "Let's burn Amber!!!" by joking that they should instead do "a drowning test"; in 2016 he tweeted that Depp was "the sweetest, kindest, gentlest man"; since 2022 he has said they had not spoken for years and in 2026 that they have not spoken since.
claims.inference: A documented episode that shows loyalty to a friend in 2016 and later distancing; relevant to how he handles allegiance and threat.
claims.alternative: Sensitive: the texts concern a woman who alleged abuse, and Depp has denied abuse. Describe neutrally, attribute exact words, avoid motive claims, and note that court outcomes differed (UK 2020 loss; US 2022 jury largely for Depp; 2022 settlement).
claims.review_trigger: Any new court filing, statement or reporting on the Bettany-Depp texts or friendship; reassess before refresh.

claims.claim: He describes politics as occupying him "to an unhealthy extent", watched election TV "about 23 hours a day" in November 2020, and took US citizenship because he was "tired of getting shouted down on Twitter for having an opinion".
claims.inference: Vigilance about collective threat and a wish for standing within the system he lives in.
claims.alternative: Political engagement is common and circumstantial to 2016-2022 US politics.

claims.claim: He is convivial and joking in public and on set ("very jovial, jokey"; "I'm quite convivial and social"), and was surprised he copes well alone.
claims.inference: Warm, joking sociability sits alongside the anxiety; it may suggest a Seven-leaning Six, but wing is not needed for the argument.
claims.alternative: A Seven or a Nine reading leans on this register; his sustained attention to death and threat weighs against Seven.

claims.claim: He has long deprecated his own education and polish: "just a blond actor who didn't go to university"; he "faked my way" with Connelly; as a young man he felt "so uneducated" and tried to copy how others spoke; he says he "largely lied" his way into Gangster No. 1 by playing a "right ruffian".
claims.inference: Fitting in to be safe among peers (he says the street accent spared him "daily beatings") is a belonging strategy; the lie for Gangster No. 1 was a performance chosen to make "everybody feel safe enough to offer me the job".
claims.alternative: A Three would read image-shaping here; a Four, shame. His framing stresses safety and acceptance, not winning or uniqueness.

claims.claim: He wrote and directed Shelter (2014), about a homeless couple, saying it was "about judgment" and that "people are eminently forgivable"; he loves his father's phrase "There but for the grace of God, go I" for "how easily it can be us".
claims.inference: Precariousness as a moral lens: anyone can fall.
claims.alternative: Empathy for the homeless also fits his busking past and progressive politics without type.

claims.claim: Co-workers describe a precise, prepared collaborator: Elizabeth Olsen, "He's very precise, like me"; Jennifer Connelly said directing "seemed to come quite naturally to him"; Kwame Kwei-Armah praised how he built Warhol.
claims.inference: Independent named testimony on work habits that is consistent with his own preparation account.
claims.alternative: Thin, promotional testimony about craft; it says nothing direct about motive.

claims.claim: Basic biography: born 27 May 1971 in London; trained at Drama Centre London from 1990; married Jennifer Connelly on 1 January 2003 in Scotland; two children with her (Stellan and Agnes) and stepfather to her son Kai; Emmy-nominated for WandaVision (2021).
claims.inference: Metadata scaffolding only.
claims.alternative: Children's ages change; avoid ages in the article.

claims.claim: VisionQuest, which completes the WandaVision trilogy, premiered on Disney+ on 14 October 2026; Bettany describes it as about "intergenerational pain with lasers" and "grandfathers, fathers, and sons".
claims.inference: Current hook that rhymes with the father story; it should date, not carry, the argument.
claims.alternative: Promotional framing; do not claim Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars appearances, which are unconfirmed.
claims.review_trigger: VisionQuest finale and any renewal or cancellation news; official confirmation or denial of Bettany in Avengers: Doomsday (18 December 2026) or Secret Wars (2027).

claims.claim: Bettany says Marvel let him turn down work, spend time with family, direct, and get films funded, and that the Vision call came minutes after he was told his career was over.
claims.inference: The franchise became a security floor, which fits the family-first, safety-first pattern.
claims.alternative: Many actors credit franchises with financial freedom; not discriminating.
claims.review_trigger: Future statements about leaving or continuing as Vision.

claims.claim: In 2026 he described childhood as a maze: "everybody is dropped into a maze by their childhood. And the job of growing up is trying to find your way out of that maze. And I did ... a lot of therapy."
claims.inference: A late-life summary that frames growth as finding a way out with help, not as discovering a unique self.
claims.alternative: Podcast register is warm and reflective; one metaphor is weak evidence alone.

claims.claim: He took jobs he now regrets for money, and says of Master and Commander that he never thinks "Why the fuck did I do that?" - "which I can't say is true of all the movies I've made."
claims.inference: Corroborates C08 that some choices were driven by something other than artistic preference.
claims.alternative: Hindsight humour about a long filmography.

claims.claim: He says he gave up songwriting because singing his own songs left him feeling "so revealed", that acting was his "safety net" (his father's "second string to your bow"), and that acting saved him because "there was always a mask that I could hide behind" so nobody knew which parts were him.
claims.inference: A Four typically wants the true self seen and expressed; Bettany chose the art form that conceals him and framed it as a fallback for safety. This is the clearest single discriminator against the Four alternative.
claims.alternative: Ordinary stage fright about one's own songs; or Five-style privacy. He still used the work to process grief, which a Four reading can claim.

claims.claim: He calls himself "an absolute fascist about being on time", traces the habit to drama-school theatre discipline ("always building more time to be there"), and repeats Anthony Hopkins's "If you're five minutes early, you're late."
claims.inference: A thirteen-year consistent habit ("pathological fear of being late" in 2013) that functions as a buffer against things going wrong.
claims.alternative: Professional training and personal style; a One would also be strict about time, though nothing else in the record suggests a One's moral perfectionism.

claims.claim: Asked in 2026 whether the fear that each job is his last ever ends, he said "I don't think that ever ends, no. Which is really depressing," and that after a couple of months off he wonders "if anybody remembers me".
claims.inference: Continuing work insecurity at 55, after franchise success, fits the security pattern in C08 and C14.
claims.alternative: A Three reading (needing to be seen) or ordinary actor insecurity; the hosts said they feel the same.

claims.claim: Bettany believes his father returned to the closet because he "had to get into heaven as a straight man so he could see his son who had died", and says his father "got really flinty" when challenged.
claims.inference: Bettany's own reading of his father's motive ties the family's two great losses together; it is his interpretation, not established fact about Thane Bettany's mind.
claims.alternative: Thane Bettany's own reasons are not on record; attribute the interpretation to Paul.

type_hypothesis.against: The Four case is real. Bettany speaks of alienation after Matthew's death ("harbouring some dreadful secret about what life is actually like"), of fans "not meeting the actual me", of himself as one of "the weirdos", and of authenticity as the lesson of his father's life. He mines his grief for performances with talismans, says acting was where he put "terrible feelings", and returned to artistic meaning after Margin Call. His anxiety and death preoccupation can also be explained by circumstance alone: a sibling's fatal fall at 16, school bullying, addiction and a precarious freelance trade, so some of the Six signal may be trauma rather than type. Much of the record is promotional interviews, where self-deprecating worry is also a British comic register.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4: a man shaped by loss who feels set apart from people who have not seen "what life is actually like", who uses acting as a container for painful feeling, who keeps returning to stories of men who could not live as themselves (Uncle Frank, Warhol, a Vision with memories he cannot feel), and who prizes authenticity above safety after watching his father retreat into the closet. Margin Call's rescue of his love for acting, the scab-picking method and the "actual me" remark all fit.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when the floor drops away. A Four turns toward the loss to deepen a distinct identity and resists trading authenticity for safety; a Six moves to secure the base and pre-empt the next threat. Across 2010-2026 Bettany repeatedly does the second, at a cost: after 9/11 he phones until he commits and calls marriage "a certainty that was new to me" (2013); at his son's birth he takes money roles to make the children safe "with dough", knowing it was exaggerated (2013, corroborated 2012/2013); after 2008 he asks "what if this thing comes tumbling down?" and calls his career what made him "feel safe" (2022); he copes with uncertainty by being "the most prepared person" and never late (2013, 2022, 2026); he distrusts fame because "What if it goes away?" (2012) and it is "untrustworthy" (2022). His fearfulness predates the brother's death ("terrified of everyone" as a bullied city boy), which weakens a trauma-only reading. The sharpest single test is how he chose his art form: a Four wants the self seen; Bettany gave up songwriting because singing his own songs left him feeling "so revealed", called acting his "safety net" (his father's "second string to your bow"), and says it saved him because it gave him "a mask that I could hide behind" so that "nobody knew which bits were me" (2026). He also says he does not want to "trade on the trauma and drama of it all". Meanwhile he deflates rather than cultivates his artist-self ("sounding like a ponce", "I'm just not good enough" at accessing emotion, "quite lazy"), which a Four rarely does. The Four-like lines cluster around grief and fame encounters rather than a sustained self-definition.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: He deliberately reopens grief for work and has played a run of men hiding their true selves, which the Six reading explains only as craft, not as choice. He is candid to the point of oversharing in interviews despite saying he is cautious, and his convivial, joking register (and early cocaine use he says he "fell in love with it the moment I started doing it") is more Seven-flavoured than the anxious core suggests. His 2016 public praise of Depp versus his later account of years without contact is not fully reconciled. The wish not to be known "definitively" could also be read as Five-style privacy, though his sociability and reliance on people and therapy argue against Five. Some 2026 podcast lines about actors never feeling fulfilled are hard to attribute to a speaker from audio alone and are not used. Wing is not established; sociability suggests 6w7 but this is optional and unproven.
